The quote is from a letter written by Blake to one of his patrons, the Reverend John Trusler, in the summer of 1799. Trusler had hired Blake to produce a series of moral artworks in the style of contemporary caricature. When Trusler criticized Blake’s artistic vision as too ‘imaginative’, Blake let Trusler know in no uncertain terms what he thought of his aesthetic sense. ‘If I am wrong, I am wrong in good company … What is grand is necessarily obscure to weak men. That which can be made explicit to the idiot is not worth my care.’ (Collected in Alfred Kazin (ed.), The Portable Blake (London: Penguin Classics, 1979).) 20.
